title: Platform-mediated news is becoming the default encounter while attention, trust, and civic interpretation fragment
source_unit: Reuters Institute for the Study of Journalism, Digital News Report 2026
geography: 48 international news markets, with age, platform, political, and trust comparisons

denominator.unit: international news markets in the Digital News Report survey

platform_news_use.unit: percent of respondents using social media and video networks for news

owned_news_use.unit: percent using news organisations' own websites and apps for news

main_source.unit: percent identifying social media and video networks as their main source of news

observations.method: Reuters Institute Digital News Report 2026, based on a YouGov survey of almost 100,000 respondents across 48 markets.
observations.uncertainty: Cross-market survey estimates describe reported news behavior and attitudes, not passive exposure, algorithmic causality, or actual political action; market samples and online survey modes affect comparability.
observations.subgroup: News users by age, market, political leaning, platform, education, and degree of interest in news.
observations.counterinterpretation: Platform use can still deliver journalism from established providers and may broaden access even when it weakens direct publisher relationships.

denominator.unit: respondents in the Digital News Report longitudinal comparison

platform_only_news.unit: percent using only social media and video networks for news in 2026

platform_only_change.unit: percent using only social media and video networks for news in 2020

casual_users.unit: percent described as casual or passive news users in 2026, up from 16 percent in 2021

observations.method: Reuters Institute repeated cross-market survey questions on news interest, frequency, and source mix.
observations.uncertainty: Self-reported frequency and source use do not reveal whether low-intent encounters change beliefs, discussion, voting, protest, or other behavior.
observations.subgroup: Casual users, people encountering news while doing other online activities, younger audiences, and people disengaging from direct news sources.
observations.counterinterpretation: Passive encounter may still expose people to important information and can sometimes prompt later search, discussion, or action.

observations.period: 2026; trust, misinformation concern, and platform reliance

denominator.unit: international news markets reporting trust and misinformation attitudes

overall_trust.unit: percent saying they trust news most of the time

social_news_trust.unit: percent saying they trust news on social media most of the time

ai_news_trust.unit: percent saying they trust news from AI chatbots most of the time

fake_news_concern.unit: percent concerned about fake or misleading news online

observations.method: Reuters Institute survey measures of trust in news overall and by source, plus concern about online misinformation.
observations.uncertainty: Trust and concern are subjective evaluations; they may reflect political identity, institutional conditions, media content, or broader social anxiety rather than source accuracy alone.
observations.subgroup: Users of social media, video networks, AI chatbots, traditional news, and groups divided by political leaning and market context.
observations.counterinterpretation: Low trust can reflect healthy skepticism; high trust does not prove accurate understanding or protection from manipulation.

denominator.unit: respondents aged 18-24 and wider age groups in the multi-market survey

young_main_source.unit: percent of 18-24-year-olds whose main news route is social media, video networks, or AI chatbots

ai_weekly_news.unit: percent using AI chatbots for news weekly in 2026, up from 7 percent year-on-year

observations.method: Reuters Institute age-stratified survey comparisons of news sources, AI use, and online video consumption.
observations.uncertainty: Age differences do not identify life-cycle versus cohort effects, and reported source preference does not establish exposure quality, political learning, or collective action.
observations.subgroup: Gen Z and younger adults, millennials, older audiences, video users, AI-chatbot users, and people relying on direct publisher products.
observations.counterinterpretation: Younger audiences may use multiple sources opportunistically; platform-first discovery does not imply rejection of professional journalism or stable ideological effects.

related_sources.claim: Reuters Institute Digital News Report 2026 landing page and chapter structure for global news-consumption trends.
Companion analysis of emerging AI-chatbot use for news and implications for journalism.

boundary: This record adds a platform-mediated encounter-to-trust-and-attention route. It is not passive behavioral telemetry, an algorithmic causal study, an individual political-action panel, or a claim that news exposure caused voting, protest, polarization, or belief change.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: The official Reuters Institute 2026 executive summary and report landing page were reviewed; platform use, passive exposure, trust, misinformation concern, age differences, AI use, and video-news claims were cross-checked.
